column2: But when we had gone down to the ship and the sea,
first of all we dragged the ship down into the divine sea,
and set the mast and sails in the black ship,
and taking the sheep we put them aboard, and we ourselves too
went aboard, grieving, shedding warm tears.
And for us from behind the dark-prowed ship
a fair wind that filled the sail she sent, a good companion,
Circe of the fair tresses, a dread goddess with human speech.
And we, having seen to each of the tackle throughout the ship,
sat; and the wind and the helmsman steered her.
Her sails were stretched all day as she crossed the sea;
and the sun set and all the ways were shadowed.
And she came to the limits of deep-flowing Okeanos.
There is the land and city of the Cimmerian men,
covered in mist and cloud; and never upon them
does the shining sun look down with his rays,
neither when he goes up to the starry heaven,
nor when he turns back again to earth from heaven,
but baneful night is spread over wretched mortals.
Going there we beached the ship, and took out the sheep;
and we ourselves went along by the stream of Okeanos,
until we came to the place which Circe had told of.
There Perimedes and Eurylochus held the victims;
and I, drawing my sharp sword from beside my thigh,
dug a pit, a cubit's length each way,
and around it I poured a libation to all the dead,
first with honeyed milk, then with sweet wine,
a third time with water; and I sprinkled white barley on it.
And I entreated much the strengthless heads of the dead,
promising, when I came to Ithaca, to sacrifice a barren cow, the best,
in my halls, and to fill the pyre with good things,
and to Teiresias apart to sacrifice a ram,
all black, which stands out among our flocks.
And when with vows and prayers I had entreated the tribes of the dead,
taking the sheep I cut their throats
over the pit, and the dark blood flowed; and there gathered
the spirits from Erebos of the dead who had died.
Brides and young unmarried men and much-enduring old men
and tender maidens with a heart new to grief,
and many wounded with bronze-tipped spears,
men slain in battle, with their armour bloodstained;
these many were thronging around the pit, one from here, one from there,
with a marvellous cry; and pale fear seized me.
Then I urged on my comrades and ordered them
to flay the sheep, which lay slain by the pitiless bronze,
and burn them, and pray to the gods,
to mighty Hades and dread Persephone;
and I myself, drawing my sharp sword from beside my thigh,
sat, and did not let the strengthless heads of the dead
come nearer the blood, before I had asked Teiresias.
And first came the spirit of my comrade Elpenor;
for he had not yet been buried beneath the broad-pathed earth;
for we had left his body in Circe's hall
unwept and unburied, since another toil urged us on.
I wept at the sight of him and pitied him in my heart,
and I spoke to him winged words:

Elpenor, how did you come beneath the misty gloom?
58	You have come sooner on foot than I with my black ship.
So I spoke, and he groaned and answered me with a word:

Zeus-born son of Laertes, Odysseus of many devices,
61	an evil doom of the spirit and measureless wine ruined me.
62	Lying down in Circe's hall I did not think
63	to go back down by the long ladder,
64	but fell straight off the roof; and my neck
65	was broken from the vertebrae, and my spirit went down to Hades.
66	And now I beseech you by those who are behind, who are not here,
67	by your wife and your father, who reared you when small,
68	and by Telemachus, whom you left alone in your halls;
69	for I know that going from here, from the house of Hades,
70	you will put in your well-built ship at the Aeaean island;
71	there then, lord, I bid you remember me.
72	Do not, going away, leave me behind unwept, unburied,
73	turning from me, lest I become a cause of the gods' anger against you,
74	but burn me with my armour, all that I have,
75	and heap up a mound for me on the shore of the grey sea,
76	for an unlucky man, that those to come may learn of it.
77	Fulfil this for me, and fix on the tomb the oar
78	with which I rowed in life when I was with my comrades.
So he spoke, and I answered him and said:
These things for you, unhappy man, I shall fulfil and do.
Thus we two sat, exchanging dreadful words,
I on one side holding my sword over the blood,
and on the other side the phantom of my comrade spoke much.
And there came the spirit of my dead mother,
Anticleia, daughter of great-hearted Autolycus,
whom I left alive when I went to sacred Ilios.
I wept at the sight of her and pitied her in my heart;
but not even so did I allow her, though grieving greatly,
to come nearer the blood, before I had asked Teiresias.
And there came the spirit of Theban Teiresias
holding a golden sceptre, and he knew me and spoke:

Zeus-born son of Laertes, Odysseus of many devices,
93	why now again, unhappy man, leaving the light of the sun,
94	have you come, to see the dead and the joyless place?
95	But draw back from the pit, hold away your sharp sword,
96	so that I may drink the blood and tell you the unerring truth.
So he spoke, and I, drawing back, thrust my silver-studded sword
into the sheath. And when he had drunk the dark blood,
then the blameless seer addressed me with words:

You seek a honey-sweet homecoming, glorious Odysseus;
101	but the god will make it hard for you; for I do not think
102	that you will escape the Earth-shaker, who has laid up wrath
103	in his heart, angry that you blinded his dear son.
104	But even so, though suffering evils, you may yet arrive,
105	if you are willing to restrain your own spirit and that of your comrades,
106	when first you bring your well-built ship near
107	to the island of Thrinacia, having escaped the violet sea,
108	and you find grazing the cattle and fat sheep
109	of Helios, who oversees all things and hears all things.
110	If you leave these unharmed and think of your homecoming,
111	you may yet reach Ithaca, though suffering evils;
112	but if you harm them, then I foretell destruction
113	for your ship and your comrades. And even if you yourself escape,
114	late you will return, in evil plight, having lost all your comrades,
115	on a stranger's ship; and you will find woes in your house,
116	overbearing men, who are devouring your livelihood,
117	wooing your godlike wife and offering bridal gifts.
118	But indeed you will take vengeance on their violence when you come.
119	And when you have killed the suitors in your halls
120	either by guile or openly with the sharp bronze,
121	then go, taking a well-made oar,
122	until you come to those who know nothing of the sea,
123	men who do not eat food mixed with salt;
124	nor do they know ships with crimson cheeks
125	nor well-made oars, which are the wings of ships.
126	And I shall tell you a very clear sign, nor will it escape you:
127	when another traveller, meeting you,
128	says that you have a winnowing-fan on your glorious shoulder,
129	then fixing the well-made oar in the ground,
130	and offering fair sacrifices to lord Poseidon,
131	a ram and a bull and a boar, mounter of sows,
132	go back home and offer holy hecatombs
133	to the immortal gods who hold the broad heaven,
134	to all in order. And death shall come to you from the sea,
135	a very gentle one, such as will slay you
136	worn out with sleek old age; and around you the people
137	will be prosperous. These things I tell you unerringly.
So he spoke, and I answered him and said:

Teiresias, these things the gods themselves have spun.
140	But come, tell me this and recount it truly:
141	I see here the spirit of my dead mother;
142	and she sits silent near the blood, and her own son
143	she has not dared to look in the face nor speak to.
144	Tell me, lord, how could she recognize me as I am?
So I spoke, and he at once answered me and said:

An easy word I shall tell you and put in your mind.
147	Whichever of the dead who have died you allow
148	to come near the blood, he will tell you truly;
149	but to whomever you begrudge, he will go back again.
So saying, the spirit of lord Teiresias went into the house of Hades
when he had spoken the oracles.
But I stayed there steadfastly, until my mother
came and drank the dark blood; and at once she knew me,
and lamenting spoke to me winged words:

My child, how have you come beneath the misty gloom
156	while alive? It is hard for the living to see these things.
157	For between are great rivers and dread streams,
158	Okeanos first, which it is not possible to cross
159	on foot, unless one has a well-built ship.
160	Do you now come here wandering from Troy
161	with ship and comrades a long time? And have you not yet come
162	to Ithaca, nor seen your wife in your halls?
So she spoke, and I answered her and said:

My mother, need brought me down to Hades
165	to consult the spirit of Theban Teiresias;
166	for I have not yet come near Achaea, nor yet set foot
167	on our land, but always have I wandered, having misery,
168	since the time I first followed divine Agamemnon
169	to Ilios of the fine horses, to fight with the Trojans.
170	But come, tell me this and recount it truly:
171	What doom of grievous death overcame you?
172	Was it a long sickness, or did Artemis the archer
173	come upon you with her gentle shafts and slay you?
174	And tell me of my father and son, whom I left,
175	whether my honour still rests with them, or some other
176	man already holds it, and they say I shall not return.
177	And tell me of my wedded wife's purpose and mind,
178	whether she remains by her child and keeps everything safe,
179	or whether already the best of the Achaeans has married her.
So I spoke, and my lady mother at once answered:

Indeed she remains, with an enduring heart,
182	in your halls; and miserable for her always
183	the nights and days wear away as she sheds tears.
184	Your fair honour no one yet holds, but undisturbed
185	Telemachus tends the estates and feasts at equal banquets,
186	which it is fitting for a man who administers justice to provide;
187	for all invite him. And your father stays there
188	in the country, and does not go down to the city. He has no beds,
189	bedclothes and cloaks and shining blankets,
190	but in winter he sleeps where the slaves are in the house,
191	in the dust near the fire, and wears bad clothes on his skin;
192	but when summer comes and flourishing autumn,
193	everywhere on the slope of his vineyard
194	lowly beds are strewn of fallen leaves.
195	There he lies grieving, and great sorrow he nurses in his heart
196	longing for your return, and grievous old age comes upon him.
197	For so I too perished and met my fate;
198	neither did the keen-sighted archer in my halls
199	come upon me with her gentle shafts and slay me,
200	nor did any sickness come upon me, which especially
201	with hateful wasting takes the spirit from the limbs;
202	but longing for you and your counsels, glorious Odysseus,
203	and your gentle kindness robbed me of my honey-sweet life.
So she spoke, and I, pondering in my mind, wished
to embrace the spirit of my dead mother.
Three times I rushed, and my heart bade me embrace her,
and three times from my hands, like a shadow or a dream,
she flew. And sharp grief grew ever more in my heart,
and I spoke to her winged words:

My mother, why do you not wait for me, who am eager to embrace you,
211	so that even in Hades, throwing our dear arms around each other,
212	we two may take our fill of chilling lamentation?
213	Or is this some phantom that august Persephone
214	has sent me, so that I may groan still more, lamenting?
So I spoke, and my lady mother at once answered:

Alas, my child, ill-fated beyond all men,
217	Persephone, daughter of Zeus, does not deceive you at all,
218	but this is the way of mortals, when one dies;
219	for the sinews no longer hold the flesh and bones,
220	but the strong force of blazing fire
221	destroys them, as soon as the spirit leaves the white bones,
222	and the spirit, like a dream, flits away and hovers.
223	But long to reach the light as quickly as you can; and know all this,
224	so that you may tell it afterwards to your wife.
Thus we two exchanged words; and the women
came, for august Persephone had urged them,
all who were wives and daughters of the best men.
And they gathered in crowds around the dark blood,
but I took counsel how I might question each.
And this seemed to my heart the best plan:
drawing my long-edged sword from beside my stout thigh,
I did not let them all drink the dark blood at once.
And they came on one after another, and each
told her lineage; and I questioned them all.
There indeed I saw first Tyro of noble father,
who said she was the offspring of blameless Salmoneus,
and said she was the wife of Cretheus son of Aeolus;
she loved a river, the divine Enipeus,
who is by far the most beautiful of rivers that flow upon the earth,
and she used to go to the fair streams of Enipeus.
In his likeness the earth-holder, the Earth-shaker,
lay with her at the mouths of the eddying river;
and a dark wave stood around them, like a mountain,
arched, and hid the god and the mortal woman.
And he loosed her maiden girdle, and poured sleep over her.
But when the god had accomplished the works of love,
he clasped her hand, and spoke a word and addressed her:

Rejoice, woman, in our love; and as the year rolls round
249	you will bear splendid children, since the couches
250	of the immortals are not barren; and you must tend and rear them.
251	Now go to your house, and hold back, and do not name me;
252	but I am Poseidon, the Earth-shaker.
So saying he dived beneath the surging sea.
And she, conceiving, bore Pelias and Neleus,
who both became strong servants of great Zeus,
both; Pelias lived in spacious Iolcus
rich in flocks, and the other in sandy Pylos.
And the other sons she bore to Cretheus, queen of women,
Aeson and Pheres and Amythaon, delighting in chariots.
And after her I saw Antiope, daughter of Asopus,
who boasted that she had slept even in the arms of Zeus,
and she bore two sons, Amphion and Zethus,
who first founded the seat of seven-gated Thebes,
and built towers, for without towers they could not
dwell in spacious Thebes, strong though they were.
And after her I saw Alcmene, wife of Amphitryon,
who bore Heracles of the steadfast mind, the lion-hearted,
having lain in the arms of great Zeus;
and Megara, daughter of high-spirited Creon,
whom the son of Amphitryon, of ever unwearied might, had as wife.
And I saw the mother of Oedipus, fair Epicaste,
who did a great deed in the ignorance of her mind,
marrying her own son; and he, having killed his father,
married her; and at once the gods made it known to men.
But he in lovely Thebes, suffering pains,
ruled the Cadmeans through the baneful counsels of the gods;
and she went to the house of Hades the strong gatekeeper,
having fastened a steep noose from the high roof,
seized by her grief; and to him she left behind
many pains, as many as a mother's Furies bring to pass.
And I saw very beautiful Chloris, whom once Neleus
married for her beauty, when he gave countless bridal gifts,
the youngest daughter of Amphion son of Iasus,
who once ruled mightily in Minyan Orchomenus;
and she was queen in Pylos, and bore him splendid children,
Nestor and Chromius and proud Periclymenus.
And after them she bore mighty Pero, a wonder to mortals,
whom all the neighbours wooed; and Neleus would not
give her to anyone who did not drive off the curved, broad-browed cattle
from Phylace, of the might of Iphicles,
hard ones; and these the blameless seer alone undertook
to drive off; but a hard fate from the god bound him,
and grievous bonds and country herdsmen.
But when the months and days were completed
as the year came round again and the seasons came on,
then the might of Iphicles released him,
when he had told all the oracles; and the will of Zeus was fulfilled.
And I saw Leda, the wife of Tyndareus,
who bore to Tyndareus two stout-hearted sons,
Castor, tamer of horses, and Polydeuces, good with his fists.
both of whom the life-giving earth holds, though alive;
who even beneath the earth, having honour from Zeus,
on one day live in turn, and on the next again
are dead; and they have obtained honour equal to the gods.
And after her I saw Iphimedeia, wife of Aloeus,
who said that she had lain with Poseidon,
and she bore two sons, but short-lived they were,
godlike Otus and far-famed Ephialtes,
whom the grain-giving earth nourished as the tallest
and by far the most beautiful, after famous Orion;
for at nine years they were nine cubits
in breadth, and in height they became nine fathoms.
These threatened the immortals in Olympus
to raise the din of tumultuous war.
They strove to set Ossa upon Olympus, and on Ossa
leafy Pelion, that heaven might be climbable.
And they would have accomplished it, if they had reached the measure of youth;
but the son of Zeus, whom fair-haired Leto bore, destroyed
them both, before the down beneath their temples
had bloomed, and covered their chins with flowering beard.
And Phaedra and Procris I saw, and fair Ariadne,
daughter of baleful-minded Minos, whom once Theseus
from Crete to the hill of sacred Athens
was bringing, but had no joy of her; for before that Artemis killed her
in sea-girt Dia, on the testimony of Dionysus.
And Maera and Clymene I saw, and hateful Eriphyle,
who took precious gold for her dear husband.
But all of them I could not tell nor name,
as many wives and daughters of heroes as I saw;
for before that immortal night would be spent. But it is also time
to sleep, either going to the swift ship to my comrades
or here; and my sending will be the care of the gods and of you."
So he spoke, and they all became hushed in silence,
held by enchantment through the shadowy halls.
And among them white-armed Arete began to speak:

Phaeacians, how does this man appear to you
337	in form and size and in his balanced wits within?
338	And he is my guest, but each of you shares the honour;
339	therefore do not hasten to send him off, nor
340	curtail his gifts when he is in such need; for you have many
341	possessions lying in your halls by the gods' favour.
And among them spoke also the old hero Echeneus,
who was the eldest of the Phaeacian men:

Friends, not wide of the mark nor of our opinion
345	does the wise queen speak; but obey.
346	And on Alcinous here depend both deed and word.
And Alcinous answered him and spoke:

This word shall be so indeed, if I
349	live and rule over the Phaeacians, lovers of oars;
350	and let the guest, though greatly longing for his return,
351	nevertheless endure to stay until tomorrow, until I
352	complete the whole gift; and his sending will be the care of all
353	the men, and most of mine; for mine is the power in the land.
And answering him wise Odysseus said:

Lord Alcinous, most distinguished of all people,
356	if you bade me stay here even for a year,
357	and hasten my sending and give splendid gifts,
358	even that I should wish, and it would be much better
359	to come to my dear fatherland with a fuller hand;
360	and I should be more respected and dearer to all
361	men who might see me returned to Ithaca.
And Alcinous answered him and spoke:

O Odysseus, we do not at all judge you, looking at you,
364	to be a deceiver and a cheat, such as many
365	the black earth feeds, men scattered widely,
366	fashioning lies from where no one could even see;
367	but on you is a grace of words, and within are good wits.
368	And you have told your tale as skilfully as a singer,
369	the grievous troubles of all the Argives and of yourself.
370	But come, tell me this and recount it truly,
371	whether you saw any of your godlike comrades, who with you yourself
372	followed to Ilios and there met their fate.
373	And this night is very long, immeasurable; and it is not yet time
374	to sleep in the hall; but tell me your marvellous deeds.
375	I could even endure until divine dawn, if you
376	would dare to tell in the hall your troubles.
And answering him wise Odysseus said:

Lord Alcinous, most distinguished of all people,
379	there is a time for many tales, and a time also for sleep;
380	but if you still desire to hear, I would not
381	begrudge you these, and to tell other more piteous things,
382	the sufferings of my comrades, who perished afterwards,
383	who escaped the Trojans' groaning battle-cry,
384	but perished on their return through the will of an evil woman.
385	But when holy Persephone had scattered here and there
386	the spirits of the women,
387	there came the spirit of Agamemnon son of Atreus
388	grieving; and around him others were gathered, as many as with him
389	in the house of Aegisthus died and met their fate.
390	And he knew me at once, when he had drunk the dark blood;
391	and he wept shrilly, shedding warm tears,
392	stretching out his hands towards me, eager to reach me;
393	but he no longer had steadfast strength, nor any vigour,
394	such as there was before in his supple limbs.
395	I wept at the sight of him and pitied him in my heart,
396	and I spoke to him winged words:
397	'Most glorious son of Atreus, lord of men, Agamemnon,
398	what doom of grievous death overcame you?
399	Did Poseidon overcome you in your ships,
400	rousing the dreadful blast of grievous winds?
401	Or did hostile men harm you on the land
402	as you were cutting off cattle and fair flocks of sheep,
403	or fighting for a city and for women?'
404	So I spoke, and he at once answered me and said:
405	'Zeus-born son of Laertes, Odysseus of many devices,
406	neither did Poseidon overcome me in my ships,
407	rousing the dreadful blast of grievous winds,
408	nor did hostile men harm me on the land,
409	but Aegisthus, contriving death and fate for me,
410	killed me with my accursed wife, having called me to his house,
411	having feasted me, as one kills an ox at the manger.
412	So I died by a most pitiable death; and around me my other comrades
413	were slain without pause, like white-tusked swine,
414	which in the house of a rich man of great power
415	are slaughtered for a wedding or a club-feast or a flourishing banquet.
416	Already you have met the slaughter of many men,
417	killed in single combat and in strong battle;
418	but you would most have lamented in your heart at that sight,
419	how around the mixing-bowl and the laden tables
420	we lay in the hall, and the whole floor ran with blood.
421	And most piteous I heard the voice of Priam's daughter,
422	Cassandra, whom treacherous Clytaemnestra killed
423	over me; and I, lifting my hands to the ground,
424	dying, beat them about my sword; but the dog-eyed woman
425	turned away, nor did she dare, though I was going to Hades,
426	to close my eyes with her hands and press my mouth together.
427	So there is nothing more dreadful and shameless than a woman,
428	who puts such deeds in her mind;
429	such a shameful deed as that one contrived,
430	devising murder for her wedded husband. Indeed I thought
431	that I should come home welcome to my children and my servants;
432	but she, knowing exceeding evil,
433	poured shame on herself and on the women yet to be hereafter,
434	even on one who is virtuous.'
435	So he spoke, and I answered him and said:
436	'Alas, indeed wide-seeing Zeus has hated the offspring of Atreus
437	terribly, from the beginning, through the counsels of women;
438	for Helen's sake many of us perished,
439	and for you Clytaemnestra prepared guile while you were far away.'
440	So I spoke, and he at once answered me and said:
441	'Therefore now do not ever you either be gentle to your wife;
442	do not tell her every word that you know well,
443	but tell one part, and let another be hidden.
444	But for you, Odysseus, there shall be no murder from your wife;
445	for very prudent and well versed in her mind in counsels
446	is the daughter of Icarius, wise Penelope.
447	Indeed we left her a young bride
448	when we went to the war; and a child was at her breast,
449	an infant, who now, I suppose, sits among the count of men,
450	blessed; for his dear father will see him when he comes,
451	and he will embrace his father, as is right.
452	But my wife did not even allow me to fill my eyes
453	with my son; for before that she killed me myself.
454	And another thing I shall tell you, and lay it in your mind:
455	secretly, not openly, to your dear fatherland
456	bring in your ship; since women can no longer be trusted.
457	But come, tell me this and recount it truly,
458	whether you have heard anywhere of my son still living,
459	perhaps in Orchomenus or in sandy Pylos,
460	perhaps with Menelaus in broad Sparta;
461	for divine Orestes has not yet died upon the earth.'
462	So he spoke, and I answered him and said:
463	'Son of Atreus, why do you ask me this? I do not know at all
464	whether he lives or is dead; and it is wrong to speak windy words.'
465	Thus we two stood exchanging dreadful words,
466	grieving, shedding warm tears;
467	and there came the spirit of Achilles son of Peleus
468	and of Patroclus and of blameless Antilochus
469	and of Ajax, who was best in looks and in build
470	of the other Danaans after the blameless son of Peleus.
471	And the spirit of the swift-footed grandson of Aeacus knew me,
472	and lamenting spoke winged words:
473	'Zeus-born son of Laertes, Odysseus of many devices,
474	hardy man, what greater deed will you yet devise in your mind?
475	How did you dare to go down to Hades, where the dead
476	dwell without sense, phantoms of worn-out mortals?'
477	So he spoke, and I answered him and said:
478	'O Achilles son of Peleus, far the best of the Achaeans,
479	I came for the need of Teiresias, in case he might tell
480	some counsel how I might reach rugged Ithaca;
481	for I have not yet come near Achaea, nor yet set foot
482	on our land, but always have evils. But of you, Achilles,
483	no man is more blessed, neither before nor after.
484	For before, when you were alive, we Argives honoured you equal to the gods,
485	and now again you rule mightily among the dead
486	being here; therefore do not grieve at having died, Achilles.'
487	So I spoke, and he at once answered me and said:
488	'Do not, I pray, speak smoothly to me of death, glorious Odysseus.
489	I would rather be a labourer on the land, serving another,
490	a man without lot, who had no great livelihood,
491	than rule over all the perished dead.
492	But come, tell me the tale of my noble son,
493	whether he followed to war to be a leader, or not.
494	And tell me of blameless Peleus, if you have heard anything,
495	whether he still holds honour among the many Myrmidons,
496	or whether they dishonour him throughout Hellas and Phthia,
497	because old age holds him in hands and feet.
498	For I am no helper beneath the rays of the sun,
499	being such as I once was in broad Troy
500	when I slew the best of the host, defending the Argives;
501	if such I could come, even for a short time, to my father's house,
502	I would make my strength and my invincible hands hateful to any
503	who do him violence and keep him from honour.'
504	So he spoke, and I answered him and said:
505	'Of blameless Peleus I have indeed heard nothing,
506	but of your dear son Neoptolemus
507	I shall tell you the whole truth, as you bid me;
508	for I myself brought him in a hollow balanced ship
509	from Scyros to the well-greaved Achaeans.
510	Indeed whenever we took counsel about the city of Troy,
511	he always spoke first and did not miss in his words;
